what_happened.line: The Select Board approved the Water District's earth removal permit with the Planning Director's conditions plus set hours of operation and warning signs.
The board authorized the town manager to renegotiate the Casella contract, with a cap per ton, because recycling will now cost the town.
Annual 2019 license renewals were approved, with all of one licensee's tavern licenses made contingent on payment of outstanding taxes.
The board agreed to send a letter of support for the open space and recreation plan and appointed two members to the cable committee.
A Chapter 61B land conversion was set for the January 8 agenda; the board is unlikely to exercise its right of first refusal.

why_it_matters: Recycling moves from a service the town was paid for to a per-ton cost, and that cost lands on the general fund, which is mostly funded by taxes.
The Water District permit lets excess fill leave the headquarters site under conditions on hours and signage, which affects truck traffic on nearby roads.
License fees have not been raised since 1995, so any increase the board takes up would change what local license holders pay.
watch_next: January 8 Select Board agenda: the Chapter 61B conversion and the board's first-refusal decision.
January 15 workshop with historical groups on town buildings; January 29 is held in reserve.

what_happened.line: The Select Board set one FY2019 tax rate for all property classes, with a residential factor of 1.0, pending state Department of Revenue approval.
The board voted to stay at four members until the regular election rather than call a special election for the vacant seat.
The board named a vice chair and a clerk after a member's resignation, and ratified two DPW appointments.
The Charter Review Committee seat was filled by a contested vote; the minutes record the outcome as not audible.
The board approved 2019 alcohol license renewals as read and agreed to skip the December workshop, aiming for a joint January facilities meeting.

why_it_matters: A single rate means homes and businesses are taxed at the same rate per an amount as heard of value, and rising valuations mean the average residential bill still goes up even as the rate falls.

Staying at four members leaves the board without a fifth vote on any split decision until the regular election, in exchange for avoiding a special election that was estimated at a few thousand dollars.
The fire pumper truck was flagged in capital planning as needing a full appropriation to order, a request residents may be asked to vote on at Town Meeting.
watch_next: State Department of Revenue approval of the FY2019 tax rates.
A joint January meeting on facilities with the historic commission, historical society and APDC, and a future agenda item on the open space endorsement request.

The board continued the tax classification hearing to December 4 at 7:05 pm, pending preliminary state Department of Revenue certification.
The board acted on earth removal permits: permit 15 was extended by a passed vote, and the votes on permits 14, 16, 17, 27, 30 and 32 were not audible.
The board heard the DPW pavement and drainage report and a first-quarter report in which revenues and expenditures were described as on track.
The meeting opened with tributes to departing selectman Bob Ebersol, and the board later entered executive session on litigation.

why_it_matters: The tax classification hearing sets how the tax burden is split between homeowners and businesses, so the December 4 continuation is where the rate decision for residents' bills is still open.
The road work discussed is paid by debt exclusion money and a yearly road budget increase, so it touches street repairs and the tax bill.
With a vacant board seat and reorganization pending, the board's membership and leadership are not yet settled.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted to authorize final payment to the school project's general contractor and to pursue the design engineers for the heating system and the roof.
The board learned that town counsel advised withholding the contractor's final payment was not possible; members disputed the heating and roof problems.
The board ratified the town manager's appointment of a full-time police officer, effective March 30, 2018.
The board reviewed draft Annual Town Meeting articles, including a snow and ice deficit amendment, the FY19 capital plan, and sewer, solid waste, water and cable budgets.
On economic development, the board leaned toward meeting the Agricultural Commission next and reached no resolution; the vote on the pregnant workers policy was not audible.

why_it_matters: The final payment closes out the middle/high school project, and pursuing the design engineers is the route by which the town may seek to recover the cost of heating and roof problems, which would otherwise fall on the town budget, mostly taxes.
The draft Town Meeting articles are the budget items residents will be asked to vote on, including the capital plan and the sewer, water and solid waste budgets.
watch_next: Town counsel's answer on conflict of interest and rule of necessity for the Hickory Hills article, before Town Meeting.
Scheduling of the Agricultural Commission meeting on economic development and of the parks, agriculture and conservation workshops.

Neighbors spoke against the license on parking, noise, septic and safety grounds, while the host said donations were optional and the event was not a business.
The board took up common victualler licenses, a 90-day closure for the Bootlegger and a ratification of an assistant town clerk; counts were not audible.
A motion to send a letter opposing House bill 4075, with a minor change, was made; the count was not audible.
The board agreed to take the tax-increase concern up at the budget meeting, then went into executive session.

why_it_matters: The Holman Street hearing shows how the board applies its licensing authority to private events that draw neighbors' complaints, which bears on events in residential areas.
The tax-increase concern was deferred to the budget meeting, so any effect on a tax bill will be discussed there rather than decided here.

what_happened.line: The Select Board renewed the bond anticipation note for the middle/high school project, as presented, by a passed vote.
The Board agreed to hold the final school-project payment warrant, and a member crossed out the signature, pending building committee answers on leaks.
The Board opened the warrant for the May 5, 2018 annual Town Meeting by a passed vote.
A resident asked why the note is being renewed; officials said final bonding awaits the MSBA audit and that authorized borrowing exceeded actual borrowing.
The Board ratified a senior property tax work-off committee appointment and heard a Council on Aging mission and goals presentation.

why_it_matters: The school building project is still not finally financed, so the town carries short-term note borrowing and its interest cost until the MSBA audit sets the final reimbursement and bonding.
Holding the last contractor payment over reported leaks and punch-list items bears on whether the town pays in full for work that residents will own and maintain.
The May Town Meeting warrant is now open, and the budget calendar for the coming year will lead to votes residents are asked to take.
watch_next: The building committee's answers on school leaks at the next Select Board meeting, and the held final payment warrant.
The Finance Committee meetings targeted for January 25 and March 29 for a possible quorum.

what_happened.line: The Select Board spent most of the meeting in a workshop with state-funded consultants on the town's Complete Streets policy; no budget votes were taken.
Consultants said the town can apply for state construction funds for projects on a prioritization list, and a board member questioned whether Chapter 90 funds are enough.
Residents named problem spots for sidewalks, crosswalks and speeding, including Lancaster Avenue, Highland Street and the route from Turkey Hill Road toward the ball fields.
Consultants will compile project lists, issue a public survey in the coming weeks, and draft a prioritization plan with design and construction cost estimates.
The board read the routine warrants; the vote result is not audible in the captions. The next meetings were noted for January 16 and January 23.

why_it_matters: Sidewalk and crosswalk projects that reach the prioritization list may qualify for state construction money, but the town pays for design and for yearly upkeep such as striping, which falls on the town budget, mostly taxes.
Staff suggested tying small projects to roads already funded for paving, so which streets get repaved may shape where sidewalk work happens.
watch_next: A public survey on Complete Streets projects, expected in the coming weeks.
The consultants' prioritization plan with cost estimates, and the next Select Board meetings on January 16 and January 23.

The board voted to support and sign a regional technical assistance application for a business brochure and a permitting guidebook.

The board aimed to hold an executive session on the town manager's salary at the January 16th meeting.
The town manager is to provide a periodic log of road moratorium waiver requests.

why_it_matters: The OPEB policy sets how much of the town's free cash goes toward retiree health costs each year, which affects how much is left for other uses and how large the long-term liability grows.
Because the deposit depends on a Town Meeting request, residents may be asked to vote on it, and the policy's wording decides whether that request is expected every year.
